metadata.title: Steps towards a classification of $C^r$-generic dynamics close to homoclinic points

extraction_notes.note: The paper is an announcement: almost all results (Theorems 1-13, Propositions) are stated without proof; only Proposition 6.8 has a sketched proof environment. Derivations between announced results are given as one-sentence 'X implies Y' remarks, extracted as short proof nodes.
problem or open_problem: 'characterize ...' research questions in Problem environments; kept as problem (author's word), resolved partly by Theorems 1-2.
Scholium typed proposition; the starred Fact typed claim (author's observation, not cited); Remark 2.2 retyped theorem/external as it states the cited adapted-metrics result of [G1].
The counterexample construction of Section 6.1 is given in prose; taken as an example node from 'Let $f$ be' to the end of its assumption list.

Proof sketches carry rigor semi_formal per the proof-sketch rule, but rigor is not allowed on proofs; put semi_formal on the result proved by the sketch instead, with no alternative flag since no full proof exists.
The dependency diagram of results in Section 1.3 and all figures (\input pdf_tex) are not in the source.

Informal restatements of theorems in the introduction and abstract are recorded as also_stated_at of the formal nodes, not as nodes; motivational prose about cited results only mentioned (Romero, Moreira, Bonatti-Diaz-Kiriki) has no nodes.

nodes.name: residual set
nodes.statement: By large sets, we mean open and dense sets, or {\em residual} sets, that is, a countable intersection of open and sense subsets.
differentia: a countable intersection of open and sense subsets

nodes.name: C^r-generic diffeomorphisms
nodes.statement: In this paper we study the dynamics of $C^r$-generic diffeomorphisms, that is, the dynamics of residual subsets of diffeomorphisms of ${Diff}^r(M)$, where $M$ is a compact Riemannian manifold and $r\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: C^r-generic dynamics means the dynamics of residual subsets of Diff^r(M), M a compact Riemannian manifold.

nodes.name: hyperbolic diffeomorphisms
nodes.statement: There exists an open set of diffeomorphisms -- now called hyperbolic diffeomorphisms -- whose dynamics has been extensively studied and are now well understood, thanks in particular to the spectral decomposition theorem of Smale (see for instance~\cite{BDV}).

nodes.name: Non-density of hyperbolic diffeomorphisms (Abraham-Smale; Newhouse)
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, hyperbolic diffeomorphisms fail to be dense in ${Diff}^1(M)$ when $\dim M\geq 3$~\cite{AS}, and in ${Diff}^2(M)$ on surfaces~\cite{N1}.
assumptions: $\dim M\geq 3$
conclusions: hyperbolic diffeomorphisms fail to be dense in ${Diff}^1(M)$ when $\dim M\geq 3$~\cite{AS}, and in ${Diff}^2(M)$ on surfaces~\cite{N1}

nodes.name: Palis' density conjecture
nodes.statement: For $r\geq 1$, any diffeomorphism in ${Diff}^r(M)$ is either approximated by hyperbolic ones or by diffeomorphisms exhibiting a homoclinic tangency or a heterodimensional cycle.
assumptions: $r\geq 1$
conclusions: any diffeomorphism in ${Diff}^r(M)$ is either approximated by hyperbolic ones or by diffeomorphisms exhibiting a homoclinic tangency or a heterodimensional cycle

nodes.name: Newhouse region
nodes.statement: That open set is often called a {\em Newhouse region}.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Newhouse phenomena close to homoclinic tangencies and heteroclinic cycles

nodes.name: Turaev's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$. There is a Newhouse region $C^r$-close to a homoclinic tangency if and only if that tangency is not volume-hyperbolic.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Newhouse phenomena close to homoclinic tangencies and heteroclinic cycles
also_stated_at: As seen in the introduction, Turaev conjectured that volume-hyperbolicity is the only obstruction to the occurrence of Newhouse phenomena $C^r$-close to a homoclinic tangency.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$
conclusions: There is a Newhouse region $C^r$-close to a homoclinic tangency if and only if that tangency is not volume-hyperbolic.
equivalent_conditions: There is a Newhouse region $C^r$-close to a homoclinic tangency
nodes.label: c.turaev

nodes.name: basic set
nodes.statement: A {\em basic set} for a difeomorphism $f$ is a compact hyperbolic set, that is transitive and locally maximal.
also_stated_at: A {\em basic set} is a transitive locally maximal invariant hyperbolic set.

nodes.name: index of a basic set
nodes.statement: Its {\em index} (also {\em stable index}) is the dimension of its stable manifold.

nodes.name: mechanism (Bonatti)
nodes.statement: Bonatti~\cite{B} proposed to call "mechanism" any of the two following dynamical objects: \begin{itemize} \item robust tangencies: a basic set $K$ such that for any small $C^r$-perturbation of the dynamics, the stable and unstable laminations of the continuation of $K$ meet non-transversally, \item robust cycles: a pair of basic sets $K$ and $L$ such that, for any small $C^r$-perturbation, the unstable lamination of one meets the stable lamination of the other. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Bonatti's mechanisms: robust tangencies of a basic set, and robust cycles between two basic sets.

nodes.name: Bonatti's conjecture
nodes.statement: He conjectured that there is an open and dense subset of diffeomorphisms that are either hyperbolic, or exhibit one of these two mechanism.
conclusions: there is an open and dense subset of diffeomorphisms that are either hyperbolic, or exhibit one of these two mechanism

nodes.name: extended list of mechanisms
nodes.statement: We propose to extend the list of mechanisms to include: \begin{itemize} \item periodic points with {\em non-simple Lyapunov spectrum}: periodic points at which the derivative of the first return map has a pair of eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) with same modulus, \item tangencies between different basic sets: a pair of basic sets of same index such that the stable lamination of one meets non-transversally the unstable lamination of the other. More generally: "bundle tangencies", where a plane of a strong-stable or center-stable distribution on the stable manifold of one basic set intersects in a non-generic position a plane of a strong-unstable or center-unstable distribution on the unstable manifold of the other basic set. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Adds periodic points with non-simple Lyapunov spectrum and (bundle) tangencies between basic sets to the mechanisms.

nodes.name: cycles of saddles: non-domination iff mechanical non-domination
nodes.statement: A cycle of saddle points has no domination of index $i$ if and only if it has mechanically no domination of index $i$.
conclusions: A cycle of saddle points has no domination of index $i$ if and only if it has mechanically no domination of index $i$.
equivalent_conditions: A cycle of saddle points has no domination of index $i$
it has mechanically no domination of index $i$

nodes.name: Wen-Gourmelon theorem (tangencies vs domination)
nodes.statement: Wen~\cite{W} and the author~\cite{G2} proved that a homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has no domination of same index as $P$ if and only if there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a homoclinic tangency related to $P$.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Extensions of classical $C^1$-dynamics results to the $C^r$-topology through mechanisms
conclusions: a homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has no domination of same index as $P$ if and only if there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a homoclinic tangency related to $P$
equivalent_conditions: a homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has no domination of same index as $P$
there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a homoclinic tangency related to $P$

nodes.name: C^1 creation of bundle tangencies
nodes.statement: It is easy to deduce, with the techniques of~\cite{BCDG}, that if the homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has no domination of index $i$ then there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a bundle tangency of index $i$ related to $P$.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Extensions of classical $C^1$-dynamics results to the $C^r$-topology through mechanisms
also_stated_at: With the techniques of~\cite{BCDG}, one deduces that if the homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has no domination of index $i$ then there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a bundle tangency of index $i$ related to $P$.
assumptions: the homoclinic class of a saddle $P$ has  no domination of  index  $i$
conclusions: there is a $C^1$-perturbation that creates a bundle tangency of index $i$ related to $P$

nodes.name: Newhouse phenomena
nodes.statement: Given a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$ and an $f$-invariant set $\Lambda$, we will say that {\em Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$} if the following holds: for any open set $U$ containing $\Lambda$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $f$ is in the closure of ${\mathcal U}$, \item $C^r$-generic diffeomorphisms in ${\mathcal U}$ have infinitely many sinks or sources, by restriction to $U$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Newhouse phenomena occur near Λ if for every neighborhood U, f is accumulated by an open set whose generic elements have infinitely many sinks/sources in U.

nodes.name: characterization of Newhouse phenomena
nodes.statement: Given an $f$-invariant set $\Lambda$, characterize the occurrence of Newhouse phenomena $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$ by the dynamical properties of the restriction $f_{|\Lambda}$.
nodes.label: p.newh

nodes.name: characterization of dynamical phenomena close to an invariant set
nodes.statement: Given an $f$-invariant set $\Lambda$, characterize the dynamical phenomena (for instance homoclinic tangencies, wild dynamics, universal dynamics, viral dynamics, etc...) that occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$ by the dynamical properties of the restriction $f_{|\Lambda}$.
nodes.label: p.general

nodes.name: hyperbolic set
nodes.statement: An invariant set $\Lambda$ is {\em hyperbolic} if there is a $Df$-invariant continuous splitting $TM_{|\Lambda}=E^s\oplus E^u$ of the tangent bundle such that there is some positive iterate of the dynamics that contracts (resp. dilates) by a factor $\lambda>1$ all nonzero vector of $E^s$ (resp. $E^u$).
differentia: there is a $Df$-invariant continuous splitting $TM_{|\Lambda}=E^s\oplus E^u$ of the tangent bundle such that there is some positive iterate of the dynamics that contracts (resp. dilates) by a factor $\lambda>1$ all nonzero vector of $E^s$ (resp. $E^u$)

nodes.name: index of a hyperbolic set
nodes.statement: The {\em index} of $\Lambda$ is the dimension of its stable bundle.

nodes.name: dominated splitting
nodes.statement: The notion of hyperbolic splitting is naturally weakened to that of dominated splitting: a $Df$-invariant continuous splitting $TM_{|\Lambda}=E_1\oplus \ldots \oplus E_k$ into constant-dimensional vector bundles is {\em dominated} if there exists $\lambda>1$ and an iterate $N>0$ such that for any point $x\in \Lambda$, for any pair of unit vectors $u,v\in E_i, E_{i+1}$ in consecutive bundles and above $x$, we have $$\|Df^N(u)\|<\lambda^{-1}\|Df^N(v)\|.$$
nodes.genus: $Df$-invariant continuous splitting $TM_{|\Lambda}=E_1\oplus \ldots \oplus E_k$ into constant-dimensional vector bundles
nodes.statement_short: A splitting is dominated if some iterate expands vectors of each next bundle uniformly more than those of the previous one.

nodes.name: domination of index i
nodes.statement: A {\em domination of index $i$} on an $f$-invariant set $\Lambda$ is a dominated splitting $E\oplus F$ such that the bundle $E$ has dimension $i$.
also_stated_at: An invariant set is {\em dominated of index $i$}, if it admits a two-bundles dominated splitting where the first bundle has dimension $i$ (see~\cref{s.preldef}).

nodes.name: volume-hyperbolic set
nodes.statement: An invariant set $\Lambda$ of a diffeomorphism $f$ is {\em volume-hyperbolic} if there exists a dominated splitting $T_\Lambda M= E^{vs}\oplus E^{c}\oplus E^{vu}$ such that the bundles $E^{vs},E^{vu}$ are non-trivial and such that volume is contracted on $E^{vs}$ and expanded on $E^{vu}$ by a factor $\lambda>1$ by some iterate of the dynamics, that is, for some $N$, for all $x\in \Lambda$, the determinants $\det(Df^N_{|E^{vs}_x})$ and $\det(Df^{-N}_{|E^{vu}_x})$ are less than $\lambda^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Λ is volume-hyperbolic if it has a dominated splitting E^vs ⊕ E^c ⊕ E^vu with volume uniformly contracted on E^vs and expanded on E^vu.

nodes.name: volume-hyperbolicity prevents sinks and sources
nodes.statement: If a set $\Lambda$ is volume-hyperbolic, clearly no sink nor source will appear by $C^1$ perturbations in a neighborhood of $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: adapted metrics for dominated splittings
nodes.statement: By~\cite{G1}, there are adapted metrics to dominated splittings: one may change the Riemannian metric on $M$ to an equivalent Riemannian metric and assume that $N=1$ in the definition of domination.
conclusions: there are adapted metrics to dominated splittings: one may change the Riemannian metric on $M$ to an equivalent Riemannian metric and assume that $N=1$ in the definition of domination

nodes.name: homoclinic tangency
nodes.statement: A {\em homoclinic tangency} is a saddle point $P$ whose stable and unstable manifold meet non-transversely at a point $x$.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
differentia: whose stable and unstable manifold meet non-transversely at a point $x$

nodes.name: homoclinic tangency related to P
nodes.statement: We say that we have a homoclinic tangency {\em related to $P$}.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: homoclinic tangency (as a compact set)
nodes.statement: By abuse of terminology, we call {\em homoclinic tangency} the compact set \begin{align*}\Lambda&=\overline{\operatorname{Orb}(x)}\\ &=\operatorname{Orb}(P)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(x). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: heteroclinic cycle
nodes.statement: A {\em heteroclinic cycle} is a pair of saddle points $P,Q$ connected through two heteroclinic points $x\in W^s(P)\cap W^u(Q)$ and $y\in W^u(P)\cap W^s(Q)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
differentia: connected through two heteroclinic points $x\in W^s(P)\cap W^u(Q)$ and  $y\in W^u(P)\cap W^s(Q)$

nodes.name: heteroclinic cycle (as a compact set)
nodes.statement: Similarly we call {\em heteroclinic cycle} the set \begin{align*} \Lambda&=\overline{\operatorname{Orb}(x)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y)}\\ &= \operatorname{Orb}(P)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(Q) \cup \operatorname{Orb}(x)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: heterodimensional cycle
nodes.statement: A {\em heterodimensional cycle} is a particular case of heteroclinic cycle where $P$ and $Q$ have different indices.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: Newhouse theorem
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Theorem} (Newhouse~\cite{N1,N2}). {\em Let $r\geq 2$ and let $\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency on a surface. Then Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
also_stated_at: In celebrated papers of the seventies, Newhouse~\cite{N1,N2} showed that homoclinic tangencies on surfaces lead to particularly wild dynamics: nearby any smooth diffeomorphism on a surface with a homoclinic tangency, there is a residual subset of an open set of diffeomorphisms, such that any element in it displays infinitely many sinks or sources.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$
$\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency on a surface
conclusions: Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: sectionally dissipative
nodes.statement: In a remarkable paper, Palis and Viana extended this to higher dimension under a technical hypothesis: the $f$-invariant set $\Lambda$ is called {\em sectionally dissipative} if, either for $f$ or its inverse, volume on any $2$-plane $P$ in $T_\Lambda M$ is exponentially contracted by positive iterations.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: Palis-Viana theorem
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Theorem} (Palis-Viana~\cite{PV}). {\em Let $r\geq 2$ and let $\Lambda$ be a sectionally dissipative homoclinic tangency. Then Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$. }
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
also_stated_at: That result was extended in the nineties to higher dimension by Palis and Viana~\cite{PV} for saddles that satisfy a technical condition "sectional dissipativity" that implies in particular that the saddle has stable or unstable index $1$.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$
$\Lambda$ be a sectionally dissipative homoclinic tangency
conclusions: Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (sharp dichotomy volume-hyperbolicity vs Newhouse phenomena)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency or a heteroclinic cycle for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$. One has a sharp dichotomy: \begin{itemize} \item either $\Lambda$ is volume-hyperbolic, \item or Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
also_stated_at: \noindent {\bf Theorem.} {\em Let $r>1$. There is a sharp dichotomy: a homoclinic tangency or a heteroclinic cycle is \begin{itemize} \item either volume-hyperbolic, \item or there is a Newhouse region $C^r$-close to it. \end{itemize} }
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
$\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency or a heteroclinic cycle for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$
conclusions: either $\Lambda$ is volume-hyperbolic,
or  Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$
nodes.statement_short: Near a homoclinic tangency or heteroclinic cycle, either the set is volume-hyperbolic or Newhouse phenomena occur (C^r, r>=2).
nodes.label: t.lambda

nodes.name: homoclinic class
nodes.statement: Recall first that the {\em homoclinic class} of a saddle $P$ is defined by the closure of the transverse intersections of the stable and unstable manifolds of $P$: $$\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)=\overline{W^s(f,P)\pitchfork W^u(f,P)}.$$
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
also_stated_at: Recall that the homoclinic class of a saddle point $P$ is the closure of the transverse intersections of the stable and unstable manifolds of $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Hom(P,f) is the closure of the transverse homoclinic intersections of P.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (robustization of non-domination)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency or a heteroclinic cycle containing a saddle $P$ for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$. Assume that $\Lambda$ has no dominated splitting of any index in a set $I\subset {\mathbb N}$. Then one can make simultaneously robust those non-dominations by a $C^r$-perturbation: in any neighborhood ${\mathcal V}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ of $f$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {\mathcal V}$ of diffeomorphisms $g$ such that the homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P_g,g)$ of the continuation $P_g$ of $P$ has no domination of any index $i\in I$.
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
$\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency or a heteroclinic cycle containing a saddle $P$  for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$
$\Lambda$ has no dominated splitting of any index in a set $I\subset {\mathbb N}$
conclusions: in any neighborhood ${\mathcal V}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ of $f$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {\mathcal V}$ of diffeomorphisms $g$ such that the homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P_g,g)$ of the continuation $P_g$ of $P$ has no domination of any index $i\in I$
nodes.statement_short: Non-dominations of a tangency/cycle can be made simultaneously C^r-robust on the homoclinic class of the continued saddle.
nodes.label: t.robustization

nodes.name: Addendum to Theorems 1 and 2 (Eulerian unions of saddles)
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Addendum to \cref{t.lambda,t.robustization}:} {\em both theorems still hold if the homoclinic tangency or heterodimensional cycle $\Lambda$ is replaced by a union $$\Lambda=\bigcup_{1\leq j\leq n}\operatorname{Orb}(P_j) \cup \bigcup_{1\leq j\leq m}\operatorname{Orb}(x_j)$$ where each $P_j$ is a saddle point, so that: \begin{itemize} \item the $\alpha$-limit (resp. $\omega$-limit) of each point $x_j$ is one of the orbits $\operatorname{Orb}(P_k)$, \item if we define an oriented graph $\Gamma$ so that each $\operatorname{Orb}(P_j)$ is a vertex and each $\operatorname{Orb}(x_j)$ is an edge from $\alpha(x_j)$ to $\omega(x_j)$, then that graph is Eulerian, that is, there is a closed path that goes through each edge once and only once (see \cref{f.grapheeulerienselles}). \end{itemize}}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles
assumptions: each $P_j$ is a saddle point
the $\alpha$-limit (resp. $\omega$-limit) of each point $x_j$ is one of the orbits $\operatorname{Orb}(P_k)$
that graph is Eulerian
conclusions: both theorems still hold if the homoclinic tangency or heterodimensional cycle $\Lambda$ is replaced by a union
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 1 and 2 hold for unions of saddle orbits and connecting orbits whose associated graph is Eulerian.

nodes.name: Theorems 1-2 extend to C^{1+alpha} and heteroclinic combinations
nodes.statement: We point out that these theorems \begin{itemize} \item also hold in $C^{1+\alpha}$ topologies; this is discussed in \cref{s.C1alpha}. \item hold for even more general sets $\Lambda$, namely, for heteroclinic combinations of basic sets under a similar Eulerian condition, which happens to be generic. This is discussed in \cref{s.moregenerallambda}. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: Eulerian condition is essential
nodes.statement: The Eulerian condition in the addendum is essential. It can not be replaced by a weaker strong connectivity condition, as the counter-example of \cref{s.counterex} shows (see also \cref{f.counterex3}).
nodes.section: 2.2 2.1 for homoclinic tangencies and heterodimensional cycles

nodes.name: epsilon-pseudo orbit
nodes.statement: An {\em $\epsilon$-pseudo orbit} is a sequence $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ in $M$ such that the distance from $f(x_i)$ to $x_{i+1}$ is less than $\epsilon$.
differentia: the distance from $f(x_i)$ to $x_{i+1}$ is less than $\epsilon$

nodes.name: chain relation
nodes.statement: We write $x${\SMALL$\vdash\!\dashv$}$y$ if, for all $\epsilon>0$, there exist $\epsilon$-pseudo-orbits of length $>1$ from $x$ to $y$ and from $y$ to $x$.

nodes.name: chain-recurrent set
nodes.statement: The {\em chain-recurrent set} is the set ${\mathcal C}(f)$ of points $x$ such that $x${\SMALL$\vdash\!\dashv$}$x$.

nodes.name: chain relation is an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: The relation {\SMALL$\vdash\!\dashv$} is an equivalence relation on ${\mathcal C}(f)$.
conclusions: The relation {\SMALL$\vdash\!\dashv$} is an equivalence relation on ${\mathcal C}(f)$.

nodes.name: chain-recurrence class
nodes.statement: The {\em chain-recurrence class ${\mathcal C}(x,f)$} of $x\in {\mathcal C}(f)$ is the equivalence class of $x$.

nodes.name: chain-recurrent invariant set
nodes.statement: An $f$-invariant set $\Sigma\subset {\mathcal C}(f)$ is called {\em chain-recurrent} if for all $x,y\in \Sigma$, for all $\epsilon>0$, there exist $\epsilon$-pseudo-orbits in $\Sigma$ from $x$ to $y$ and from $y$ to $x$.

nodes.name: classes as pointed sets
nodes.statement: If a point $P$ is a saddle then the chain-recurrence and homoclinic classes of $P$ will actually be identified to pointed sets: \begin{align*}{\mathcal C}(P,f)&:=\bigl({\mathcal C}(P,f),P\bigr)\\ \operatorname{Hom}(P,f)&:=\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(P,f),P\bigr). \end{align*}

nodes.name: cycle of basic sets
nodes.statement: A {\em cycle of basic sets} is a cyclic sequence $(K_\ell,x_\ell)_{\ell\in {\mathbb Z}/n{\mathbb Z}}$ where the $K_\ell$ are basic sets -- not necessarily of same index -- and $x_i$ is an intersection point of the unstable lamination of $K_\ell$ and the stable one of $K_{\ell+1}$.

nodes.name: mechanical obstruction to domination
nodes.statement: We call {\em mechanical obstruction} to domination of index $i$ any of the following: \begin{itemize} \item a periodic point $Q$ of period $p$ such that the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_d$ of the derivative $Df^p$ at $Q$, counted with multiplicity and ordered by increasing moduli, satisfy $|\lambda_i|=|\lambda_{i+1}|$. \item a {\em tangency}, that is, a pair of basic sets $K,L$ of index $i$ whose stable and unstable bundles meet non-transversely, or more generally, a {\em bundle tangency of index $i$}, which we define precisely in \cref{s.bundtang}: a plane of a strong-unstable or center-unstable distribution on the unstable manifold of $K$ intersects non-generically a plane of a strong-stable or center-stable distribution on the stable manifold of $L$, so that domination of index $i$ is prevented. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A mechanical obstruction to domination of index i: a periodic point with |λ_i|=|λ_{i+1}|, or a (bundle) tangency of index i between basic sets.

nodes.name: mechanically no domination of index i
nodes.statement: We say that the chain-recurrent class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle $P$ has {\em mechanically no domination of index $i$} if there is a cycle of basic sets that contains $P$ and a mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$.
also_stated_at: We will say that the chain-recurrence class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle $P$ has {\em mechanically no domination of index $i$} if $P$ is in a cycle of basic hyperbolic sets that contains a mechanism -- either a periodic point with non-simple Lyapunov spectrum or a tangency/bundle tangency -- preventing domination of index $i$, as depicted in~\cref{f.cyclemech}.

nodes.name: pointed chain-recurrence classes
nodes.statement: Two chain-recurrence classes ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ and ${\mathcal C}(Q,f)$ may coincide as subsets of $M$, but one may have mechanically no domination of some index while the other not. This is not an abuse of terminology if, as said previously, we consider chain-recurrent classes to be pointed sets.

nodes.name: Fact: known robust non-dominations are mechanical
nodes.statement: In all known examples, $C^1$- or $C^r$-robust obstructions to domination on the chain-recurrent class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle (see~\cite{N1,N2,PV,GST1,GST3,BD}, among other works) are locally openly and densely mechanical.
also_stated_at: All known examples of homoclinic classes/chain-recurrence classes robustly without domination of some index $i$, are obtained through mechanisms.
conclusions: In all known examples, $C^1$- or $C^r$-robust obstructions to domination on the chain-recurrent class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle (see~\cite{N1,N2,PV,GST1,GST3,BD}, among other works) are locally openly and densely mechanical.

nodes.name: non-dominations are generically mechanical

nodes.name: Bonatti-Diaz-Pujals theorem
nodes.statement: In a landmark paper of $C^1$-generic dynamics, Bonatti, Diaz and Pujals~\cite{BDP} showed that, $C^1$-generically, if a homoclinic class $\Lambda=\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ has no domination of any index, then it is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks and sources.
also_stated_at: By a famous result by Bonatti, Diaz and Pujals~\cite{BDP}, $C^1$-generically, if a homoclinic class has no domination, then it is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (C^r Bonatti-Diaz-Pujals under mechanical non-domination)
nodes.statement: For any integer $r\geq 1$, for any diffeomorphism $f$ in a residual subset ${\mathcal R} \subset {Diff}^r(M)$, if the chain-recurrent class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle $P$ has mechanically no domination of any index, that is: if, for any index $1\leq i<d$, there is a cycle of basic sets that contains the saddle $P$ and either \begin{itemize} \item a periodic point $Q$ of period $p$ such that the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,...,\lambda_d$ of the derivative $Df^p$ at $Q$, counted with multiplicity and ordered by increasing moduli, satisfy $|\lambda_i|=|\lambda_{i+1}|$, \item or a non-transverse intersection point of the stable and unstable laminations of to two basic sets $K,L$ of index $i$ (possibly $K=L$), \item or, more generally a bundle tangency of index $i$, as defined later in~section~\ref{s.bundtang}, \end{itemize} then the homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources.
also_stated_at: \noindent {\bf Theorem}{\bf .} {\em Let $r\geq 1$. Given a $C^r$-generic diffeomorphism, if the chain-recurrence class of a saddle $P$ has mechanically no domination of any index, then the homoclinic class of $P$ is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources.}

$f$ in a residual subset ${\mathcal R} \subset {Diff}^r(M)$
the chain-recurrent class ${\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle $P$ has mechanically no domination of any index
conclusions: the homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources.
nodes.statement_short: C^r-generically, a mechanically non-dominated (every index) chain-recurrence class has its homoclinic class accumulated by sinks or sources.

nodes.statement: Note first that if an invariant set $K$ has a dominated splitting $TM_K=E\oplus F$ of some index $i$, that is, the bundle $\dim(E)$ has constant dimension $i$, then the center unstable bundle $F$ is uniquely extended to a bundle $\tilde{F}$ above the unstable set $$W^u(K)=\{x\in M, \alpha(x)\subset K\}$$ that is $Df$-invariant and locally continuous, that is, continuous by restriction to a local unstable set $$W^u_\epsilon(K)=\{x\in W^u(K) \mbox{ s.t. } \forall n\in {\mathbb N}, \mathrm{dist}(f^{-n}(x), K)<\epsilon\},$$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Symmetrically, the center stable bundle $E$ is uniquely extended to a $Df$-invariant and locally continuous bundle $\tilde{E}$ above the stable set $W^s(K)$.

nodes.name: bundle tangency
nodes.statement: A {\em bundle tangency} is the data of \begin{itemize} \item a point $x\in M$ \item two dominated splittings $TM_{|\alpha(x)}=E^\alpha\oplus F^\alpha$ and $TM_{|\omega(x)}=E^\omega\oplus F^\omega$ on the $\alpha$- and $\omega$-limits of $x$, such that the extended bundles $\tilde{F}^\alpha$ and $\tilde{E}^\omega$ are not in generic position at $x$, that is, both following conditions are met: \begin{align} &d_T=\dim(\tilde{F}^\alpha_x\cap \tilde{E}^\omega_x)>0,\\ &T_xM\neq \tilde{F}^\alpha_x\oplus \tilde{E}^\omega_x . \end{align} \end{itemize}

nodes.name: homoclinic tangency as a bundle tangency

If the unstable manifold meets the stable one tangently to that foliation at some point $x$, then there is at $x$ a bundle tangency of indices $1$ and $2$ related to $P$.

nodes.name: robust bundle tangency of index i

nodes.name: properties of heteroclinic classes

nodes.name: characterization of non-volume-hyperbolicity
nodes.statement: A compact invariant set $\Lambda$ of a diffeomorphism $f$ is not volume-hyperbolic if and only if, given the finest dominated splitting $$TM_{|\Lambda}=E^1\oplus ... \oplus E^k$$ above $\Lambda$, there exists a Riemannian metric on $M$ and a point $x\in \Lambda$ such that \begin{itemize} \item either volume is not contracted on $E^1_x$ by any positive iterate of the dynamics, that is, for any $n\in {\mathbb N}$, $$\bigl|\det Df^n_{|E^1_x}\bigr|\geq 1.$$ \item or volume is not contracted on $E^k_x$ by any negative iterate of the dynamics, that is, for any $n\in {\mathbb N}$, $$\bigl|\det Df^{-n}_{|E^k_x}\bigr|\geq 1.$$ \end{itemize}

nodes.name: mechanically not volume-hyperbolic
nodes.statement: The chain-recurrent class $\Lambda={\mathcal C}(P,f)$ of a saddle $P$ for a diffeomorphism $f$ is {\em mechanically not volume-hyperbolic} if, given the finest dominated splitting \begin{align*}T_\Lambda M=E^1\oplus ... \oplus E^k\end{align*} above $\Lambda$, there exists a point $x$ in the heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$ of $P$ such that \begin{itemize} \item either the bundle $E^1$ is mechanically without dominated splitting and the sequence $$\bigl|\det Df^n_{|E^1_x}\bigr|, \quad n\in {\mathbb N}$$ is not bounded from above, \item or the bundle $E^k$ is mechanically without dominated splitting and the sequence $$\bigl|\det Df^{-n}_{|E^k_x}\bigr|, \quad n\in {\mathbb N}$$ is not bounded from above. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: C(P,f) is mechanically not volume-hyperbolic if an extreme bundle of the finest dominated splitting is mechanically non-dominated with unbounded volume growth at a point of Het(P,f).

nodes.name: bundle mechanically without dominated splitting

conclusions: a homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ is not volume-hyperbolic if and only if it is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources.
equivalent_conditions: a homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ is not volume-hyperbolic
it is the Hausdorff limit of a sequence of sinks or sources

nodes.name: Question 6.1 (non-volume-hyperbolicity and Newhouse phenomena)
nodes.statement: Does the absence of volume-hyperbolicity on a compact chain-recurrent set $\Lambda$ imply that Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$ ?
nodes.section: 6 Extensions of t.lambda,t.robustization to other sets $\Lambda$
nodes.label: q.lambda

nodes.name: non-dominated chain-recurrent set far from Newhouse phenomena (construction)
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a diffeomorphism with two saddles $P$ and $Q$ of stable indices $1$ and $2$, respectively, such that the unstable manifold of $Q$ intersects that of $P$ at a point $x$, and the unstable manifold of $P$ intersects the stable one of $Q$ at two points $y_1$ and $y_2$. Assume moreover that \begin{itemize} \item there is a three-bundles dominated splitting on $\{P,Q\}\cup \operatorname{Orb}(x)$, \item there is a bundle tangency of index $i$, and only $i$, at the heteroclinic point $y_i$, for $i=1,2$, \item the saddles $P$ and $Q$ are not sectionally dissipative, that is, if $\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\lambda_3$ are the Lyapunov exponents at $P$ (resp. $Q$), then \begin{align*} \lambda_1+\lambda_2&<0\\ \lambda_2+\lambda_3&>0. \end{align*} \item the points $y_i$ are separated by the strong-stable (resp. strong-unstable) manifold, within the stable (resp. unstable) manifold of $Q$ (resp. $P$). \item if we denote by $E^{cs}_x$ the center-stable half plane in $T_xM$ whose positive iterates converge to the center-stable half plane at $P$ tangent to the half unstable manifold containing $y_1$, and by $E^{cu}_x$ the center-unstable half plane at $x$ whose negative iterates converge to the center-unstable half plane at $Q$ tangent to the half unstable manifold containing $y_2$, then we have $$E^{cs}_x\cap E^{cu}_x=\{x\}.$$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 6.1 An example of a non-dominated chain-recurrent set, far from Newhouse phenomena
nodes.statement_short: Two saddles of indices 1 and 2 in dimension 3 with heteroclinic connections carrying bundle tangencies of single indices, not sectionally dissipative.

nodes.name: Claim 6.1 (no sinks or sources near the counterexample)
nodes.statement: There exist a neighborhood ${\mathcal U}$ of $f$ in ${Diff}^1(M)$ and a neigborhood $U$ in $M$ of the chain-recurrent set $$\Lambda=\{P,Q\}\cup \operatorname{Orb}(x)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y_1)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y_2),$$ such that for any diffeomorphism $g\in {\mathcal U}$, each periodic point in $U$ is neither a sink nor a source.
nodes.section: 6.1 An example of a non-dominated chain-recurrent set, far from Newhouse phenomena
conclusions: for any diffeomorphism $g\in {\mathcal U}$, each periodic point in $U$ is neither a sink nor a source

nodes.name: no Newhouse phenomena near the counterexample
nodes.statement: In particular, there is no Newhouse phenomena $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.
nodes.section: 6.1 An example of a non-dominated chain-recurrent set, far from Newhouse phenomena
conclusions: there is no Newhouse phenomena $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$

nodes.name: idea of the proof of Claim 6.1
nodes.statement: The idea of the proof of the claim is as follows: if a periodic orbit $R$ is created close to $\Lambda$ by $C^1$-perturbations, then because of the geometry of $\Lambda$ it cannot pass both close to $y_1$ and close to $y_2$. As a consequence there is a strong domination of index either $1$ or $2$ along $R$. The absence of sectional dissipativity then prevents that $R$ be a sink or a source.
nodes.section: 6.1 An example of a non-dominated chain-recurrent set, far from Newhouse phenomena
nodes.statement_short: Geometric argument: created periodic orbits cannot visit both y_1 and y_2, so they are dominated of index 1 or 2; lack of sectional dissipativity excludes sinks/sources.

nodes.name: path in a directed graph
nodes.statement: Recall that a {\em path} in a directed graph is an alternating sequence of vertices and connecting edges.

nodes.name: strongly connected directed graph
nodes.statement: A directed graph is called {\em strongly connected} if there exists a path from any vertex to any other.

nodes.name: heteroclinic graph
nodes.statement: A {\em heteroclinic graph} $\Gamma$ for a diffeomorphism $f$ is a directed graph, not necessarily finite, such that: \begin{itemize} \item each of its vertices is a chain-recurrent hyperbolic set, \item each edge from vertex $K$ to vertex $L$ is an orbit whose $\alpha$-limit and $\omega$-limit are subsets of $K$ and $L$, respectively, \end{itemize}
differentia: each of its vertices is a chain-recurrent hyperbolic set
each edge from vertex $K$ to vertex $L$ is an orbit whose $\alpha$-limit and $\omega$-limit are subsets of $K$ and $L$, respectively

nodes.name: support of a heteroclinic graph
nodes.statement: The {\em support} of a heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$, denoted by $\mathrm{supp} \Gamma$, is the union of the edges and vertices of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: overlapping vertices allowed
nodes.statement: We allow two vertices to have nonempty intersection. This may bring some technical difficulties (see \cref{p.gathering}, for instance), but it allows the following nice example:

nodes.name: heteroclinic class as support of a heteroclinic graph
nodes.statement: By definition, any heteroclinic class is the support of a strongly connected heteroclinic graph. Note that the vertices of that heteroclinic graph cannot be chosen to be pairwise disjoint, in general.

nodes.name: heteroclinic graph mechanically without domination
nodes.statement: A heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$ with support $\Lambda$ is {\em mechanically without domination of index $i$} if so is $\Lambda$, that is, if $\Lambda$ contains a mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$.

nodes.name: heteroclinic graph mechanically not volume-hyperbolic
nodes.statement: As seen in \cref{s.volhyp}, it is natural to say that $\Gamma$ is {\em mechanically not volume-hyperbolic} if, given the finest dominated splitting \begin{align*}T_{\Lambda} M=E^1\oplus ... \oplus E^k\end{align*} there exists a point $x\in \Lambda$ such that \begin{itemize} \item either the bundle $E^1$ is mechanically without domination and the sequence $$\bigl|\det Df^n_{|E^1_x}\bigr|, \quad n\in {\mathbb N}$$ is not bounded from above, \item or the bundle $E^k$ is mechanically without domination and the sequence $$\bigl|\det Df^{-n}_{|E^k_x}\bigr|, \quad n\in {\mathbb N}$$ is not bounded from above. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: circuit
nodes.statement: A {\em circuit} in a directed graph is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex, and that does not go twice through the same edge.
differentia: starts and ends at the same vertex
does not go twice through the same edge

nodes.name: Eulerian directed graph
nodes.statement: A directed graph is called {\em Eulerian} if for any finite subset of edges, there exists a circuit that goes through each of those edges.

nodes.name: Eulerian graphs are strongly connected
nodes.statement: This implies in particular that the graph is strongly connected.
conclusions: the graph is strongly connected

nodes.name: Theorem 10 (Newhouse phenomena near Eulerian heteroclinic graphs)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $\Lambda\subset M$ be the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that is mechanically not volume-hyperbolic, then Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
$\Lambda\subset M$ be the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that is mechanically not volume-hyperbolic
conclusions: Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.
nodes.label: t.volhyp

nodes.name: Corollary of Theorem 10 (mechanically non-dominated Eulerian graphs)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer and let $\Lambda\subset M$ be the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that has mechanically no dominated splitting, then Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
$\Lambda\subset M$ be the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that has mechanically no dominated splitting
conclusions: Newhouse phenomena occur $C^r$-close to $\Lambda$.
nodes.label: c.homcor

nodes.name: Theorem 1 and its addendum from Theorem 10
nodes.statement: The other all-important particular case is that if the vertices of a finite Eulerian heteroclinic graph are periodic points, then one has a sharp dichotomy between volume hyperbolicity and Newhouse phenomena: this is the addendum to \cref{t.lambda} in~\cref{s.turaevconj}. A homoclinic tangency and a heterodimensional cycle, as defined in \cref{s.turaevconj}, are the supports of finite Eulerian heteroclinic graphs (see \cref{f.graphecycletangence}), therefore we get \cref{t.lambda}.
nodes.statement_short: Tangencies, cycles and Eulerian unions of saddles are supports of finite Eulerian heteroclinic graphs; apply Theorem 10.

nodes.name: Proposition 6.3 (Eulerian hypothesis is generic)
nodes.statement: There exists a residual set ${\mathcal R}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ of diffeomorphisms $f$ such that any heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$ is the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph.
conclusions: any heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$ is the support of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph.
nodes.label: p.geneulerian

nodes.name: Theorems 3 and 9 from Proposition 6.3 and Theorem 10
nodes.statement: \cref{p.geneulerian} and \cref{t.volhyp} allow to recover \cref{t.comprehensible,t.mechnovolhyp}.
nodes.statement_short: Generic heteroclinic classes support Eulerian graphs (Prop. 6.3), so Theorem 10 applies.

nodes.name: strong connectivity does not suffice
nodes.statement: One cannot replace the Eulerian hypothesis by the weaker strong connectivity hypothesis in \cref{t.volhyp}, in dimension $\geq 3$. Indeed, the set $\Lambda=\{P,Q\}\cup \operatorname{Orb}(x)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y_1)\cup \operatorname{Orb}(y_2)$ from the counterexample of \cref{s.counterex} is the support of a non-Eulerian strongly connected heteroclinic graph, depicted in \cref{f.counterex3}.

nodes.name: infinitely connected directed graph
nodes.statement: A directed graph is {\em infinitely connected} if it is strongly connected and if it remains strongly connected by removal of any finite set of edges.
differentia: remains strongly connected by removal of any finite set of edges

nodes.name: infinitely connected graphs are Eulerian
nodes.statement: We note that an infinitely connected graph is always Eulerian.
conclusions: an infinitely connected graph is always Eulerian

nodes.name: Theorem 11 implies Theorem 2
nodes.statement: We now state our result, which straightforwardly implies \cref{t.robustization}:
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 is the special case of Theorem 11 for tangencies and cycles.

nodes.name: Theorem 11 (robustization for Eulerian heteroclinic graphs)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. If a saddle $P$ of $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$ is in the support $\Lambda$ of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that has mechanically no dominated splitting of indices $i\in I$, then for any open set $U$ containing $\Lambda$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item $f$ is in the closure of ${\mathcal U}$, \item for any $g$ in ${\mathcal U}$, the continuation $P_g$ of the saddle $P$ is in an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\Delta_g$ supported in $U$, that contains infinitely many mechanical obstructions to domination of each index $i\in I$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
a saddle $P$ of $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$ is in the support $\Lambda$ of a Eulerian heteroclinic graph that has mechanically no dominated splitting of indices $i\in I$
conclusions: $f$ is in the closure of ${\mathcal U}$,

for any $g$ in ${\mathcal U}$, the continuation $P_g$ of the saddle $P$ is in an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\Delta_g$ supported in $U$, that contains infinitely many mechanical obstructions to domination of each index $i\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Mechanical non-dominations on an Eulerian heteroclinic graph become robust: nearby open set where P lies in an infinitely connected graph with infinitely many obstructions.
nodes.label: t.homcor

nodes.name: C^{1+alpha} version of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: The same way we wrote in \cref{s.C1alpha} a $C^{1+\alpha}$ version of \cref{t.robustization}, \cref{t.homcor} also admits a $C^{1+\alpha}$ version. We leave it to the reader to write its statement.

nodes.name: mechanical assumption removable for finite saddle graphs
nodes.statement: If the heteroclinic graph is finite and its vertices are saddles, one can remove the "mechanical" assumption in the hypotheses.

nodes.name: trail
nodes.statement: A {\em trail} in a directed graph $\Gamma$ is a path that does not go twice through the same edge.
differentia: does not go twice through the same edge

nodes.name: Proposition 6.7 (gathering obstructions on a trail)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$ be a diffeomorphism admitting a finite heteroclinic graph $$\Gamma=\Bigl(\{K_0,...,K_m\},\{e_1,...,e_n\}\Bigr).$$ and assume that $\gamma=(K_0,e_1,K_1,\ldots K_{k-1},e_k,K_k)$ is a trail that contains mechanical obstructions to domination of any index $i$ in a set $I$. Let $\epsilon>0$ and $U$ a neighborhood of $K_1\cup \ldots \cup K_{k-1}$. Then there is an $\epsilon$-perturbation $g$ of $f$ in ${Diff}^r(M)$ and a heteroclinic graph for $g$ $$\tilde{\Gamma}=\Bigl(\{\tilde{K}_0,...,\tilde{K}_m\},\{\tilde{e},\tilde{e}_{k+1},...,\tilde{e}_n\}\Bigr)$$ such that $g=f$ outside $U$, and \begin{itemize} \item $(\tilde{K}_0,\tilde{e},\tilde{K}_k)$ is a trail that contains mechanical obstructions of all indices $i\in I$. \item for all $0\leq \ell\leq m$, the basic set $\tilde{K}_\ell$ for $g$ is the continuation of the basic set $K_\ell$ for $f$ and retains its initial mechanical obstructions to domination, for all indices $i\notin I$.\footnote{Note that the vertices are not necessarily disjoint basic sets, which is why all the vertices, and not only vertices $K_1, \ldots ,K_{k-1}$, may loose domination of indices $i\in I$.} \item for $\ell>k$, if $e_\ell$ is an edge from $K_p$ to $K_q$, then $\tilde{e}_\ell$ is an edge from $\tilde{K}_p$ to $\tilde{K}_q$ whose hausdorff distance to $e_\ell$ is less than $\epsilon$. Moreover, for any bundle tangency at $e_\ell$, there is a bundle tangency of same indices at $\tilde{e}_\ell$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A trail carrying mechanical obstructions of indices in I can be replaced by a single edge carrying them all, keeping the rest of the graph.
assumptions: $r\geq 2$ be an integer
$f\in {Diff}^r(M)$ be a diffeomorphism admitting a finite heteroclinic graph
$\gamma=(K_0,e_1,K_1,\ldots K_{k-1},e_k,K_k)$ is a trail that contains mechanical obstructions to domination of any index $i$ in a set $I$
conclusions: there is an $\epsilon$-perturbation $g$ of $f$ in ${Diff}^r(M)$ and a heteroclinic graph for $g$
nodes.label: p.gathering

nodes.name: gathering keeps supports Hausdorff close
nodes.statement: In particular, the transformation can be done so that the Hausdorff distance between the supports of $\Gamma$ and $\tilde{\Gamma}$ is arbitrarily small.
conclusions: the transformation can be done so that the Hausdorff distance between the supports of $\Gamma$ and  $\tilde{\Gamma}$ is arbitrarily small

nodes.name: Proposition 6.8 (robustizing a loop)
nodes.statement: Fix $r>1$ and $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$. Let $\Gamma=\bigl(\{K\},\{e\}\bigr)$ be a heteroclinic graph for $f$ formed by a single loop $(K,e,K)$, and containing mechanical obstructions to domination of index $i$, for any integer $i$ in a set $I$. Then there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\in {Diff}^r(M)$ containing $f$ in its closure such that, for any $g\in {\mathcal U}$, \begin{itemize} \item there is an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\tilde{\Gamma}$ for $g$ that contains the continuation $\tilde{K}$ of $K$, \item $\tilde{\Gamma}$ contains infinitely many mechanical obstructions to domination for each index $i\in I$, \item the Hausdorff distance between the supports of $\Gamma$ and $\tilde{\Gamma}$ is less than $\epsilon$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A heteroclinic loop with mechanical obstructions becomes, for an open set of nearby g, an infinitely connected graph replicating them infinitely.
assumptions: $\Gamma=\bigl(\{K\},\{e\}\bigr)$ be a heteroclinic graph for $f$ formed by a single loop $(K,e,K)$, and containing mechanical obstructions to domination of index $i$, for any integer $i$ in a set $I$
conclusions: there is an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\tilde{\Gamma}$ for $g$ that contains the continuation $\tilde{K}$ of $K$,
$\tilde{\Gamma}$ contains infinitely many mechanical obstructions to domination for each index $i\in I$,
the Hausdorff distance between the supports of $\Gamma$ and   $\tilde{\Gamma}$ is less than $\epsilon$.
nodes.label: p.robustizing

nodes.name: Addendum to Proposition 6.8
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Addendum:} {\em If $\Gamma$ is part of a larger finite heteroclinic graph $\Delta$, for any neighborhood $U$ of $K$ there is a diffeomorphism $g\in {\mathcal U}$ arbitrarily $C^r$-close to $f$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $g$ coincides with $f$ outside $U$, \item $\Delta$ is still a heteroclinic graph for $g$, up to changing the vertices to their continuations, and up to adapting the edges adjacent to those continuated vertices, and the mechanical obstructions to domination of indices $i\notin I$ on each edge and each vertex are preserved. \end{itemize} }
assumptions: $\Gamma$ is part of a larger finite heteroclinic graph $\Delta$
conclusions: for any neighborhood $U$ of $K$ there is a diffeomorphism $g\in {\mathcal U}$ arbitrarily $C^r$-close to $f$  such that

nodes.name: Main steps of the proof of Proposition 6.8
nodes.statement: With \cref{p.gathering}, we reduce the problem to the case where $\Lambda$ is the closure of a homoclinic orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(x)$ related to a saddle $P$. \medskip Let $J$ be the set of indices of non-dominations that are visible only along the homoclinic orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(x)$, that is, through bundle tangencies at $x$. The first step of the proof is to turn the homoclinic class of $P$ non-trivial, while recovering a homoclinic orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(y)$ of $P$ with bundle tangencies of same indices. In dimension $2$, $J=\{1\}$, $\Lambda$ is a homoclinic tangency: a simple picture (see for instance~\cite{PT}) can convince the reader that a generic unfolding of the tangency leads to arbitrarily small parameters where the homoclinic class is non-trivial, and where the tangency is recovered. The same reasoning works in any dimension when $J=\{\mathrm{ind} P\}$: unfolding the tangency one recovers it for arbitrarily small parameters (see~\cite{PV,Ro}). When the set $J$ has cardinal $\geq 2$, however, a generic unfolding will not allow to recover all those non-dominations at the same time. One needs to carefully choose the unfolding. \medskip Let now $I$ be the set of indices of non-domination along the closure of $\operatorname{Orb}(y)$. Each of those non-dominations is either due to a non-simple Lyapunov spectrum at $P$, that is, eigenvalues with same moduli at $P$, or a bundle tangency at $y$. By $C^r$-perturbations, one relates the bundle tangencies to other saddles homoclinically related to $P$. One is reduced to two independent problems: given a non-trivial homoclinic class $H(P,f)$ of a saddle point $P$, \begin{enumerate} \item if $\lambda_1\leq ...\leq \lambda_d$ are the Lyapunov exponents along the saddle $P$ counted with multiplicity, find a $C^r$-perturbation of $f$ such that, for any index $i$, if $\lambda_i=\lambda_{i+1}$ then there is a saddle point $Q$ homoclinically related to the saddle $P$, at which there is robustly no dominated splitting of index $i$, thanks to a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues. \item given a bundle tangency related to $P$ of indices $i\in J$, find a $C^r$-perturbation such that for any index $i\in J$, \begin{itemize} \item if $i=\mathrm{ind} P$, there is a robust homoclinic tangency related to $P$. \item if $i\neq \mathrm{ind} P$, there is a saddle point $Q$ homoclinically related to $P$ at which there is robustly no dominated splitting of index $i$, thanks to a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate} The first problem relies on the study of finitely generated semi-groups of matrices, and how those semi-groups behave through perturbations of their generators, according to the dominated splittings that exist on the corresponding linear cocycle. The second problem is solved as follows: by perturbations of the eigenvalues at $P$ and perturbation close to the tangency, one manages to multiply bundle tangencies through topological arguments. A bundle tangency of index $i=\mathrm{ind} P$, that is, a homoclinic tangency, can be turned robust thanks to~\cite{Ro} for regularity $r\geq 2$, or to~\cite{CG} for regularity $r>1$. Then a pair of bundle tangencies of same index $i\neq \mathrm{ind}(P)$ can be perturbed to obtain a saddle point homoclinically related to $P$, with complex conjugate eigenvalues at index $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce by Proposition 6.7 to a homoclinic orbit, make the class non-trivial while recovering the tangencies, then solve two problems: equal exponents to complex eigenvalues, and multiplying/robustizing bundle tangencies.

nodes.name: Lyapunov map
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be an $f$-invariant probability measure with Lyapunov exponents $\lambda_1\leq \ldots \leq \lambda_d$, counted with multiplicity. The {\em Lyapunov map}\footnote{Bochi and Bonatti call it the {\em Lyapunov graph}, we save the word "graph" for heteroclinic graphs.} of $\mu$, identified to the tuple $\sigma(\mu)=(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_d)$, where $\sigma_i=\sum_{1\leq j\leq i} \lambda_i$, is the map: $$ \sigma(\mu)\colon \begin{cases} \{0,\ldots,d\}&\to \mathbb{R}\\ i &\mapsto \sigma_i=\sum_{1\leq j\leq i} \lambda_j \end{cases}. $$
nodes.statement_short: The Lyapunov map of μ sends i to the sum of its first i Lyapunov exponents.

nodes.name: C^r-preperiodic measure
nodes.statement: For all $r\geq 1$ and $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$, we say that an $f$-invariant probability measure $\mu$ is {\em $C^r$-preperiodic} if there exists a sequence $f_n\in {Diff}^r(M)$ converging to $f$ and a sequence $P_n$ such that $P_n$ is a periodic orbit for $f_n$ and if the corresponding sequence of periodic measures $\mu_n$ converges weakly to $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: μ is C^r-preperiodic if it is a weak limit of periodic measures of diffeomorphisms C^r-converging to f.

nodes.name: Bochi-Bonatti theorem
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Theorem} (Bochi-Bonatti~\cite[Theorem~3]{BB}){\bf .} {\em Let $\mu$ be a $C^1$-preperiodic measure for $f$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$. Let $I$ be the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is a dominated splitting of index $i$ on the support of $\mu$ (we assume that $0,d\in I$). Then, any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ can be realized as a limit of Lyapunov maps for a sequence of diffeomorphisms $f_n$ converging to $f$ in ${Diff}^1(M)$ and for a sequence of periodic measure $\mu_n\in {\mathcal M}(f_n)$ weakly converging to $\mu$.}
assumptions: $\mu$ be a $C^1$-preperiodic measure for $f$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$
$I$ be the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is a dominated splitting of index $i$ on the support of $\mu$ (we assume that $0,d\in I$)
conclusions: any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ can be realized as a limit of Lyapunov maps for a sequence of diffeomorphisms $f_n$ converging to $f$ in ${Diff}^1(M)$ and for a sequence of periodic measure $\mu_n\in {\mathcal M}(f_n)$  weakly converging to  $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Near a C^1-preperiodic measure, every convex map above its Lyapunov map, equal to it at dominated indices, is a C^1-limit of periodic Lyapunov maps.

nodes.name: Mañé's ergodic closing lemma (ergodic measures are C^1-preperiodic)
nodes.statement: Ma\~n\'e~\cite{M} proved that an ergodic measure is always $C^1$-preperiodic.
conclusions: an ergodic measure is always $C^1$-preperiodic

nodes.name: preperiodic measures are supported in chain-recurrent sets
nodes.statement: Obviously, it is necessary that the measure be supported in a chain-recurrent set.
conclusions: it is necessary that the measure be supported in a chain-recurrent set

nodes.name: measure in a chain-recurrent set that is not C^1-preperiodic
nodes.statement: The example of \cref{s.counterex} can be refined by adding a pair of saddles $R_1$ and $R_2$ along the heteroclinic connections $y_1$ and $y_2$: we get the heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$ depicted in \cref{f.counterex4}. The sum of Dirac measures $\mu=\frac{1}{2}(\delta_{R_1}+\delta_{R_2})$ is a measure whose support is in the chain-recurrent set $\Lambda=\mathrm{supp} \Gamma$. However, for the same reasons as in \cref{s.counterex}, a periodic point obtained by $C^1$-perturbations cannot go close to both $R_1$ and $R_2$. Thus $\mu$ is not $C^1$-preperiodic.

nodes.name: generic preperiodicity of measures
nodes.statement: For $r\geq 1$, there exists a $C^r$-residual set of diffeomorphisms for which any invariant measure supported in a chain-recurrent set is $C^r$-preperiodic.
assumptions: $r\geq 1$
conclusions: there exists a $C^r$-residual set of diffeomorphisms for which any invariant measure supported in a chain-recurrent set is $C^r$-preperiodic

nodes.name: measure supported in a heteroclinic class
nodes.statement: The invariant probability measure $\mu$ we now consider, instead of being $C^1$-preperiodic, is {\em supported in a heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$}, that is: $$\mu\bigl[\operatorname{Het}(P,f)\bigr]=1.$$

nodes.name: measure supported in a heteroclinic graph
nodes.statement: Likewise, we say that a probability measure $\mu$ is {\em supported in a heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$} if the support of the graph has total measure: $$\mu(\mathrm{supp} \Gamma)=1.$$

nodes.name: Theorem 12 (C^r Bochi-Bonatti on infinitely connected graphs)
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be an $f$-invariant probability measure supported in an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$. Let $I$ be the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is no mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$ on $\Gamma$ (we have $0,d\in I$). Then any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ can be realized as the limit Lyapunov map of a sequence of periodic measure $\mu_n$ converging weakly to $\mu$, for a sequence of diffeomorphisms $f_n$ converging to $f$ in ${Diff}^r(M)$. Moreover if $U$ is an open set containing the support of $\Gamma$, the sequence $(f_n,\mu_n)$ can be chosen so that $\mathrm{supp} \mu_n \subset U$ for $n$ large enough.
assumptions: $\mu$ be an $f$-invariant probability measure supported in an infinitely connected heteroclinic graph $\Gamma$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$
$I$ be the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is no mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$ on $\Gamma$ (we have $0,d\in I$)
conclusions: any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ can be realized as the limit Lyapunov map of a sequence of periodic measure $\mu_n$ converging weakly to $\mu$, for a sequence of diffeomorphisms $f_n$ converging to $f$ in ${Diff}^r(M)$.
if $U$ is an open set containing the support of $\Gamma$, the sequence $(f_n,\mu_n)$ can be chosen so that $\mathrm{supp} \mu_n \subset U$ for $n$ large enough.

nodes.name: Corollary (generic C^r Bochi-Bonatti)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 1$. There is a residual subset ${\mathcal R} \subset {Diff}^r(M)$ such that if \begin{itemize} \item $f$ is a diffeomorphism in ${\mathcal R}$, \item $\mu$ is an $f$-invariant probability measure $\mu$ supported in a heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$, \item $I$ is the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is no mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$ on $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$ -- we have $0,d\in I$ -- \end{itemize} then any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ is the limit Lyapunov map of a sequence of periodic $f$-invariant measures $\mu_n$ converging weakly to $\mu$. Moreover, that sequence can be chosen so that the supports $\mathrm{supp} (\mu_n)$ converge to the homoclinic class $\operatorname{Hom}(P,f)$ for the Hausdorff topology.

$f$ is a diffeomorphism in ${\mathcal R}$,
$\mu$ is an $f$-invariant probability measure $\mu$ supported in a heteroclinic class $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$, with Lyapunov map $\sigma\colon \{0,\ldots,d\}\to \mathbb{R}$,
$I$ is the set of integers $0\leq i\leq d$ such that there is no mechanical obstruction to domination of index $i$ on $\operatorname{Het}(P,f)$
conclusions: any convex map $\tau\geq \sigma$ coinciding with $\sigma$ at indices $i\in I$ is the limit Lyapunov map of a sequence of periodic $f$-invariant measures $\mu_n$ converging weakly to $\mu$.

nodes.name: Theorem 13 (polytope of Lyapunov maps near a homoclinic tangency)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 2$. Let $\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$. Then ${\mathcal G}(\Lambda)$ is precisely the set of possible limit Lyapunov maps: $\tau\in {\mathcal G}(\Lambda)$ if and only if there are \begin{itemize} \item a sequence of diffeomorphisms $f_n$ converging to $f$ in ${Diff}^r(M)$ \item a sequence of periodic measures $\mu_n\in {\mathcal M}(f_n)$ where the supports $\mathrm{supp} \mu_n$ converge to a subset of $\Lambda$ for the Hausdorff topology, \end{itemize} such that $\tau=\lim_{n\to \infty}\sigma(\mu_n)$. Moreover, for any open set $U\supset \Lambda$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item $f$ is in the closure $\overline{{\mathcal U}}$, \item for any diffeomorphism $g$ in a residual subset ${\mathcal R}\subset {\mathcal U}$, if $\Pi_{g_{|U}}$ is the set of Lyapunov maps of periodic measures for the restriction $g_{|U}$, then the closure $\overline{\Pi_{g_{|U}}}$ is a neighborhood in ${\mathbb R}^d$ of the polytope ${\mathcal G}(\Lambda)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 7.2 An application: polytope of realizable Lyapunov exponents along periodic orbits, close to a homoclinic tangency.
also_stated_at: We deduce a full picture of the $C^r$-generic Lyapunov exponents along periodic orbits, close to homoclinic tangencies: those asymptotically realizable vectors of Lyapunov exponents (by $C^r$-perturbations) form a convex polytope, and they are locally generically simultaneously realized. More precisely, for a generic diffeomorphism in a nearby open set of dynamics, the vectors of Lyapunov exponents along periodic orbits are dense in a neighborhood of the polytope (see \cref{s.polytope}).
assumptions: $r\geq 2$
$\Lambda$ be a homoclinic tangency for a diffeomorphism $f\in {Diff}^r(M)$
conclusions: ${\mathcal G}(\Lambda)$ is precisely the set of possible limit Lyapunov maps
for any open set  $U\supset \Lambda$, there exists an open set ${\mathcal U}\subset {Diff}^r(M)$
nodes.statement_short: Near a homoclinic tangency, the realizable limit Lyapunov maps form exactly the polytope G(Λ), and generic nearby g realize a dense set around it.

nodes.name: candidate polytope for a heterodimensional cycle
nodes.statement: If $\Lambda$ is now a heterodimensional cycle linking two saddles $P$ and $Q$, $I$ is the union of $\{0,d\}$ and the set of integers $0< i< d$ such that there is a dominated splitting of index $i$ on $\Lambda$, and $\mu,\sigma$ are the Lyapunov maps of the Dirac measures at the two saddles $P$ and $Q$ of the homoclinic cycle, then the candidate set ${\mathcal G}(\Lambda)$ in \cref{t.Lyaptang} would be the polytope formed of convex Lyapunov maps $\tau$ such that, for some $0\leq \lambda\leq 1$, \begin{itemize} \item $\tau\geq \tau_\lambda=\lambda\mu+(1-\lambda)\sigma$, \item $\tau$ coincides with $\tau_\lambda$ at indices $i\in I$. \end{itemize}

nodes.statement_short: For a heterodimensional cycle, G(Λ) is the set of convex maps above some convex combination of the two saddles' Lyapunov maps, agreeing at dominated indices.

nodes.name: Introduce J and make the homoclinic class non-trivial while recovering tangencies
nodes.statement: Let $J$ be the set of indices of non-dominations that are visible only along the homoclinic orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(x)$, that is, through bundle tangencies at $x$. The first step of the proof is to turn the homoclinic class of $P$ non-trivial, while recovering a homoclinic orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(y)$ of $P$ with bundle tangencies of same indices.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce J and make the homoclinic class non-trivial while recovering tangencies

nodes.name: Cases |J|=1 (generic unfolding works) versus |J|>=2 (unfolding must be chosen)
nodes.statement: In dimension $2$, $J=\{1\}$, $\Lambda$ is a homoclinic tangency: a simple picture (see for instance~\cite{PT}) can convince the reader that a generic unfolding of the tangency leads to arbitrarily small parameters where the homoclinic class is non-trivial, and where the tangency is recovered. The same reasoning works in any dimension when $J=\{\mathrm{ind} P\}$: unfolding the tangency one recovers it for arbitrarily small parameters (see~\cite{PV,Ro}). When the set $J$ has cardinal $\geq 2$, however, a generic unfolding will not allow to recover all those non-dominations at the same time. One needs to carefully choose the unfolding.
nodes.statement_short: Cases |J|=1 (generic unfolding works) versus |J|>=2 (unfolding must be chosen)

nodes.name: Reduce to two independent problems
nodes.statement: Let now $I$ be the set of indices of non-domination along the closure of $\operatorname{Orb}(y)$. Each of those non-dominations is either due to a non-simple Lyapunov spectrum at $P$, that is, eigenvalues with same moduli at $P$, or a bundle tangency at $y$. By $C^r$-perturbations, one relates the bundle tangencies to other saddles homoclinically related to $P$. One is reduced to two independent problems: given a non-trivial homoclinic class $H(P,f)$ of a saddle point $P$, \begin{enumerate} \item if $\lambda_1\leq ...\leq \lambda_d$ are the Lyapunov exponents along the saddle $P$ counted with multiplicity, find a $C^r$-perturbation of $f$ such that, for any index $i$, if $\lambda_i=\lambda_{i+1}$ then there is a saddle point $Q$ homoclinically related to the saddle $P$, at which there is robustly no dominated splitting of index $i$, thanks to a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues. \item given a bundle tangency related to $P$ of indices $i\in J$, find a $C^r$-perturbation such that for any index $i\in J$, \begin{itemize} \item if $i=\mathrm{ind} P$, there is a robust homoclinic tangency related to $P$. \item if $i\neq \mathrm{ind} P$, there is a saddle point $Q$ homoclinically related to $P$ at which there is robustly no dominated splitting of index $i$, thanks to a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to two independent problems

nodes.name: First problem via semigroups of matrices and linear cocycles
nodes.statement: The first problem relies on the study of finitely generated semi-groups of matrices, and how those semi-groups behave through perturbations of their generators, according to the dominated splittings that exist on the corresponding linear cocycle.

nodes.name: Second problem via multiplying tangencies and robustization (Romero, Crovisier-Gourmelon)
nodes.statement: The second problem is solved as follows: by perturbations of the eigenvalues at $P$ and perturbation close to the tangency, one manages to multiply bundle tangencies through topological arguments. A bundle tangency of index $i=\mathrm{ind} P$, that is, a homoclinic tangency, can be turned robust thanks to~\cite{Ro} for regularity $r\geq 2$, or to~\cite{CG} for regularity $r>1$. Then a pair of bundle tangencies of same index $i\neq \mathrm{ind}(P)$ can be perturbed to obtain a saddle point homoclinically related to $P$, with complex conjugate eigenvalues at index $i$.
